Docker & Kubernetes
The Complete Developer Guide
Docker
Container Engine
Kubernetes
Container Orchestration
1. What is Docker?
Docker is an open-source platform launched in 2013 that allows developers to package applications and all
their dependencies into a standardized unit called a container. A container is a lightweight, portable,
self-sufficient environment that runs the same way regardless of the host machine — whether it's your laptop, a
test server, or a cloud data center.
Before Docker, the classic problem was "It works on my machine" — code would behave differently across
environments due to OS differences, library versions, or configuration mismatches. Docker solves this by
bundling everything the app needs into one image.
2. What is Kubernetes?
Kubernetes (often abbreviated K8s) is an open-source container orchestration system originally developed by
Google, now maintained by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). While Docker creates and runs
individual containers, Kubernetes manages hundreds or thousands of containers across multiple machines —
automatically scaling, healing, and load-balancing them.
Think of it this way: Docker is the shipping container; Kubernetes is the entire shipping port that decides
where containers go, replaces broken ones, and routes traffic intelligently.

Why & Where We Use Docker and Kubernetes
3. Why Use Docker?
• Consistency: Run the exact same container in dev, staging, and production — zero environment drift.
• Isolation: Each container is sandboxed. A crash in one container doesn't affect others.
• Speed: Containers start in milliseconds (vs. minutes for VMs), boosting developer productivity.
• Portability: A Docker image runs on any OS with Docker installed — Windows, Mac, Linux, cloud.
• Microservices: Each service (auth, payments, notifications) lives in its own container, independently
deployable.
• CI/CD Pipelines: Docker integrates cleanly with Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI for automated builds
& deploys.
• Resource Efficiency: Containers share the host OS kernel — much lighter than full virtual machines.
4. Why Use Kubernetes?
• Auto-scaling: K8s automatically scales your containers up/down based on CPU, memory, or custom
metrics.
• Self-healing: If a container crashes, K8s restarts it automatically. Dead nodes? Containers are
rescheduled.
• Load Balancing: Distributes incoming traffic evenly across all healthy container instances.
• Rolling Updates: Deploy new versions with zero downtime — K8s gradually replaces old containers with
new ones.

Core Concepts You Must Know
6. Essential Docker Concepts
Concept
What It Means
Dockerfile
A text file with step-by-step instructions to build a Docker image. Every image starts from a Dockerfile.
Image
A read-only snapshot of your app + its environment. Built from a Dockerfile. Think of it as a template.
Container
A running instance of an image. You can run many containers from the same image simultaneously.
Docker Hub
The public registry (like GitHub for images) where you pull official images (nginx, postgres, node, etc.).
Volume
Persistent storage mounted into a container. Data survives even if the container is deleted.
Network
Docker's virtual network that lets containers communicate with each other securely.
Docker Compose
A YAML file to define and run multi-container apps (e.g., web app + database + cache) with one command.
Registry
A storage system for Docker images. Can be Docker Hub, AWS ECR, Google GCR, or self-hosted.

Concept
What It Means
Pod
The smallest deployable unit in K8s. A pod wraps one or more containers that share the same network/stora
Node

Cluster
A group of nodes managed by Kubernetes together as one logical computing resource.

Node
A physical or virtual machine in the cluster. Each node runs pods managed by the control plane.
Cluster
A group of nodes managed by Kubernetes together as one logical computing resource.
Deployment
Declares the desired state — e.g., 'I want 5 replicas of my web app running.' K8s maintains it.
Service
A stable network endpoint (with a fixed IP/DNS) that routes traffic to the right pods.
Namespace
A virtual partition of the cluster. Use it to separate dev/staging/prod or different teams.
ConfigMap
Store non-sensitive configuration (env variables, config files) separately from your container image.
Secret
Like ConfigMap but for sensitive data (passwords, tokens). Stored encrypted.
Ingress
Manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to services — like a smart reverse proxy inside your cluster.
kubectl
The command-line tool to talk to your Kubernetes cluster. Apply configs, check logs, scale apps.

Learning Roadmap & Sample YAML
10. Sample Dockerfile
Every Docker journey starts with writing a Dockerfile. Here's a real-world Node.js example:
FROM node:20-alpine # Start from official lightweight Node image
WORKDIR /app # Set working directory inside container
COPY package*.json ./ # Copy dependency files first (for cache efficiency)
RUN npm install # Install dependencies
COPY . . # Copy the rest of the app source code
EXPOSE 3000 # Document the port the app listens on
CMD ["node", "server.js"] # Command to run when container starts
11. Sample Kubernetes Deployment YAML
A Deployment YAML tells Kubernetes exactly what to run and how many copies to maintain:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
name: myapp-deployment
spec:
replicas: 3 # Run 3 identical pods
selector:
matchLabels:
app: myapp
template:
metadata:
labels:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
name: myapp-deployment
spec:
replicas: 3 # Run 3 identical pods
selector:
matchLabels:
app: myapp
template:
metadata:
labels: {app: myapp}
spec:
containers:
- name: myapp
image: myrepo/myapp:1.0 # Docker image to use
ports:
- containerPort: 3000

Master docker build, run, compose first — K8s will feel much more natural once you think in containers.
